client_need: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
stem: A nurse is preparing insulin for two hospitalized clients. An insulin pen assigned to Client A has medication remaining, and the nurse considers changing the needle and using the same pen for Client B. Which action is correct?

options.A: Do not use the pen for Client B because insulin pens are single-patient devices even when a new needle is attached.
options.B: Use the pen for Client B after replacing the needle because the cartridge cannot be contaminated by blood.
options.C: Use the pen for Client B if both clients have negative screening tests for bloodborne infections.
options.D: Use the pen for Client B if the outside of the pen is disinfected between injections.

rationale: A is correct. Current CDC injection-safety guidance states that insulin pens and other medication cartridges are for single-patient use only and must never be used for more than one person. Blood may be present in the pen after use, so changing the needle does not make sharing safe. B, C, and D all incorrectly assume that needle replacement, infection-screening results, or surface disinfection can convert a single-patient insulin pen into a multi-patient device.
educational_objective: Prevent bloodborne-pathogen transmission by assigning each insulin pen to one client only and never sharing the pen between clients, even when a new needle is used.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
source_document_title: Considerations for Blood Glucose Monitoring and Insulin Administration; CDC Core Infection Prevention and Control Practices
source_version_date: CDC pages dated 2024 and current as accessed 2026-08-17
